signals.reasoning: NVDA is plainly a sound enterprise: current ratio is 4.59, debt/equity is 0.15, earnings are positive throughout the record, and returns on equity are exceptional. But the defensive investor demands a margin of safety, and here the price is too rich: a P/E of 26.2 exceeds my customary 15-20 limit, and at 8.00 EPS against 9.50 BVPS the price is roughly 22 times book value. I will not call it bearish, since the balance sheet is strong and the earnings are demonstrated rather than merely hoped for, but I cannot call it bullish when so little demonstrated book value backs the quotation.

This is not my usual circle, but the numbers describe an extraordinary business: returns on equity near 84%, net margins of 64%, gross margins widening to 75%, low debt, a 4.6 current ratio, and free cash flow of $5.27 per share. Revenue is still growing 83% and the shares trade at only 26 times earnings, so a wonderful business is available at a fair—not demanding—price. The risks are semiconductor cyclicality and the sheer size required to keep compounding, but for a ten-year owner the moat and balance sheet look durable enough.

Invert: what kills this? Falling margins, rising leverage, capital-hungry growth — none present. Gross margin has widened from 56% to 75% across the history, operating margin sits at 65%, ROE is 84%, debt is a trivial 0.15 of equity, and free cash flow per share has compounded from $2.96 to $5.27 while the business buys back stock (hence the flat book value). This is a genuinely wonderful business earning monstrous returns on capital without heroic assumptions, and the numbers have been consistent and improving for three years, not one lucky quarter. At 26x trailing earnings against 83% revenue growth and doubling EPS, the price is fair, not foolish — so I'll pay up for quality, while flagging that revenue growth is decelerating from triple digits and no semiconductor franchise stays this profitable forever.
